title: Readable Code Review
eyebrow: Design for approval · changes the build plan for #468 (code preview and issue rule) · nothing redrafted yet

short.lead: Code review only becomes routine if it is easy. Today's drafts use short names like _rc and _o, pack several things into one line, and the page wraps lines in the middle of words. With this change, a check refuses unreadable code before you see it. Each step then opens with plain sentences saying what it changes, followed by short labelled blocks of code. Making the code readable is my work, not yours.
short.hint: Tap an item to see what it creates and what it needs from you.
items: A readability check on every draft
Plan mode refuses to build the page while any added line breaks a readability rule, naming the line and the rule. I fix it before you see it.

Each step opens with one plain sentence per change. Each change is a short block with its own caption, line numbers and colour, and no line breaks mid-word. Tests are folded under their plain-English names.

The code on the build plan page
From one wrapped wall of diff to plain sentences and short captioned blocks.

The step's draft is split into its changes, one block of changed lines each. Each block gets a one-sentence caption that I write, and plan mode refuses a block with no caption. Lines keep their shape: a long line scrolls sideways inside its box instead of breaking mid-word. Test code is folded under each test's plain-English name, so the first thing you read is what the step changes.

The readability check
Six rules, checked on every line a draft adds.

1. Names say what they hold, in whole words: step_size, not _s or sz. Standard words stay allowed (id, url, html, json, git, and i in a counted loop). 2. One thing per line: no semicolons joining statements, and no splitting a result into short names such as _rc, _o. 3. A condition with more than two parts becomes named yes-or-no values, such as was_refused and names_the_step. 4. Lines are at most 100 characters. 5. Every new function starts with one plain sentence saying what it does. 6. No logic inside one-line lambdas (small unnamed functions) or nested comprehensions (loops written inside a list). Plan mode refuses a draft that breaks a rule, and names the file, the line and the rule. The writing check covers Markdown and rule text.
Nothing checks how readable drafted code is.
A check that refuses unreadable drafted code, naming line and rule.
The code you review has already been made readable.
chg
The writing check
It reads the page's sentences, not its code.
The writing check reads every string on the page, code included, and flagged 379 repeated phrases in the build plan.
It skips the code views and still checks every sentence, caption and choice.
The change is in page_text, in scripts/clarity.py, which reads the page's content block. Code readability is the readability check's job.
chg
The four drafts
Rewritten to the rules, tests included.
Steps 1 to 4 use the file's existing short-name style.
Every line they add follows the six rules, and each block of changes has its caption.

Existing code around the drafts keeps its style unless the second choice says otherwise. The redrafted steps are tested as before. The full suite runs in the scratch copy, and the drafts must reproduce the tested copy exactly.
new
Risks and unknowns
What could make this cost more than it saves.

Readable code is longer. The drafts will grow by an amount I have not measured yet, and the redraft will measure it. New lines will look different from older code in the same file. The second choice decides whether that is fixed now or later. The house coding standard says a file's existing style wins. For these rules, your need to read clearly wins instead. The third choice decides how far that reaches.
No risk today.
Longer drafts, and two styles side by side in some files.
You read code that explains itself.
choices: strict
What happens when a draft breaks a readability rule?
A
The page is not built until I fix it
You never see unreadable code. The friction is mine.
B
The page is built with a warning on that line
You see the problem and decide. More for you to read.
You said friction makes review easy to skip. Option A keeps every fix on my side.
reach
How much code do the rules cover?
A
Every line a draft adds or changes
New code is readable. Older code around it is left as it is.
B
Also the whole function or test block a draft touches
Each block you read is readable throughout, but the drafts grow larger.
C
A now, plus a separate issue to make the whole plugin readable
New code now; the rest later, as its own planned work.
Option A keeps each review small. If the mix of styles bothers you while reading, option C plans the rest without making this build bigger.
where
Where should the readable-code rules apply?
A
Every project, as a house coding standard
The six rules go into the coding standards loaded in every session, so any project's code follows them.
B
Only drafts in this plugin's build plans
The rules live in the readability check alone.
Your need to read code clearly is the same in every project, so the rules should follow you there.
tick
How do you approve the code?
A
One tick per step; the reply builds itself
Each step has Looks right and Change something. When every step is ticked, the copy box holds the approval.
B
One approval for the whole plan, as now
Fewer taps, but nothing shows which steps you have read.
A tick per step makes it visible which code you have looked at, without adding anything to type.

wrapup.summary: Drafted code passes a readability check before you see it. The page then shows plain sentences, short captioned code, folded tests and a tick per step.
wrapup.changing: Plan mode gains the readability check, captions and the new view; the writing check skips code; the four drafts are rewritten to the rules.
